chapter: Setting the record straight on Hendersonia
title: Were his arrangements more modern? Collaborating on 'Sometimes I'm Happy'
summary: Horace calls modernity a matter of taste, noting King Porter Stomp swings as much as anything, and recalls finishing the brass chorus of Fletcher's 'Sometimes I'm Happy' for Goodman. They traded tunes according to feel.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: That's right. Then it goes on to say here, 'His arrangements were also more,' quote, 'modern for their time.' This -- your arrangements were more modern than Fletcher's.

That's a matter of opinion, and I'm not being -- you know, because of the fact he's my brother, but I don't know -- it all depends upon a person's taste, you know. Maybe I was given a certain style of arranging to do, which required the swing thing, but Fletcher made things like King Porter Stomp. They don't swing any more than that, man! Sometimes I'm Happy -- there's a beautiful thing he and I made together. Benny Goodman did this thing. Fletcher did it for Benny. And Fletcher had played it before in his band too -- 'Sometimes I'm Happy,' and the reed chorus was a legend, you know.

It flowed, you know. Okay, so he wrote this early in the morning. He wrote the 16 bars. So he called me upstairs, and I was asleep, and he asked me if I'd come down and finish that, and I wrote the brass chorus, where it comes in --
Well, I wrote that. I don't know if even Benny knew that until

later on, you know, that it was -- we collaborated on the thing together, unintelligible, you know, but we did things together, and then if he wanted me to do something that was a thing -- he'd always ask me, AAH, 'You want to do this tune?' Well, I'd take and play it, and I'd see if I felt it, you know, and I can play it down, you know, and if I felt the tune had a feeling -- if I had a feeling for that particular tune, I'd say, 'Yeah, I want to do this.'

But he gave me some, he said -- I'd say, 'Smack, I don't think I feel this one, because, see, I might do a corny deal on this.' unintelligible to you. He said, 'Okay, I'll take it,' you know, one of these things, but we always agreed. So it was just a matter of the way you felt about the tune. And I never wanted to write any -- this is why I loved Jimmy Dorsey, you know, because he said, 'Look, if you don't feel like doing this thing, don't do it, you know.'
